summary.text: Two events are independent if the occurrence of one does not affect the probability of the other.
Dependence is the opposite case, where the occurrence of one event does affect the likelihood of another.
For more than two events, mutual independence implies pairwise independence, but pairwise independence does not imply mutual independence.

facts.label: Default meaning
facts.value: Unqualified, independence usually means mutual independence

facts.label: Dice rolls
facts.value: A 6 on the first roll and a 6 on the second are independent

facts.label: Card draws
facts.value: Red draws are independent with replacement, dependent without it

facts.label: Zero covariance
facts.value: Two variables with covariance 0 may still be dependent

facts.label: Self-independence
facts.value: A random variable is independent of itself only if almost surely constant

items.prompt: You draw two cards from a deck and want the red-card draws to be independent. What must you do after the first draw?

options.label: Return the card before drawing again
Keep the card out of the deck
Shuffle only the remaining cards
Draw the second card faster

items.explain: With replacement the draws are independent; without it the deck has proportionately fewer red cards, so they are not.

items.prompt: Three events are independent of each other when taken two at a time. A student concludes they must be mutually independent. What is wrong?

options.label: Pairwise independence is stronger than mutual independence
Independence only ever applies to two events
Pairwise independence does not guarantee mutual independence
Mutual independence needs fewer conditions

items.explain: Mutual independence implies pairwise independence, but not the other way around.

items.prompt: Two random variables have a covariance of 0. A friend says that proves they are independent. What is the verdict?

options.label: Correct, because zero covariance defines independence
Correct, but only for real numbers
Wrong, since covariance cannot be 0
They still may not be independent

items.explain: The converse does not hold, since two random variables with covariance 0 may still be not independent.

items.prompt: Learning that event A happened changes how likely event B is. What does this say about A and B?

options.label: They are independent
They are dependent
They are mutually exclusive
They are conditionally independent

items.explain: Dependence is when the occurrence of one event does affect the likelihood of another.

items.prompt: A statistics textbook says “the events are independent” with no further wording. For a collection of events, which meaning is usually intended?

options.label: Mutual independence
Pairwise independence only
Independence of just two events
Conditional independence

items.explain: Independence without further qualification usually refers to mutual independence.

items.prompt: Saying “B’s probability is unchanged given A” sounds natural. Why is it not the preferred definition of independence?

options.label: It only works for random variables, not for events
It cannot show that A and B are truly linked
The conditional forms can be undefined for a zero-probability event
It needs three or more events before it can apply

items.explain: Conditional probabilities may be undefined if P(A) or P(B) are 0, and the preferred definition is symmetric.
